name: Caramelization
statement: Heat sugar alone and it breaks apart, browning into caramel's colour and buttery flavour.
statementAccent: browning into caramel's colour and buttery flavour
meaning: Caramelization is the browning of sugar, a process of thermal decomposition, or pyrolysis, in which sugar is heated until its molecules break down and recombine into new compounds that give the characteristic brown colour and rich, buttery, sometimes nutty flavour of caramel. It is a form of non-enzymatic browning, but unlike the Maillard reaction it involves only sugars and requires no amino acids or proteins. Caramelization is used throughout cooking, from making caramel candy and sauces to browning the top of a crème brûlée and giving colour and flavour to countless dishes. As sugar is heated past a characteristic temperature, it melts and then undergoes a cascade of reactions that produce hundreds of compounds, including flavour molecules and brown pigments. Different sugars caramelize at different temperatures, with table sugar, sucrose, browning around 170 degrees Celsius. Caramelization is a cornerstone of confectionery and cooking, prized for turning plain sugar into complex colour and taste.
mechanism: Caramelization is not a single reaction but a complex process of thermal breakdown. As sugar is heated to its caramelization temperature, it melts and its molecules begin to decompose through dehydration, fragmentation, isomerization, and polymerization, producing an array of new substances. Among the flavour compounds are diacetyl, which contributes a buttery note, and furans and related molecules that give caramel and toasty flavours. The brown colour comes from high-molecular-weight polymers formed as fragments recombine, named caramelans, caramelens, and caramelins as they grow darker and more complex. Because it depends on breaking down sugar itself, caramelization requires no amino acids, which is the key difference from the Maillard reaction. Different sugars caramelize at different temperatures: fructose caramelizes lowest, around 105 to 110 degrees Celsius, glucose around 150 degrees, sucrose around 170 degrees, and maltose higher still. Continued heating darkens the caramel and eventually leads to bitter, burnt compounds, so caramelization is a matter of controlled heating to the desired stage.

examples.text: Heating sugar until it browns produces caramel candy and sauces, the classic use of caramelization in confectionery.
The crackly brown top of a crème brûlée is made by caramelizing a layer of sugar with intense heat.
So-called caramelized onions brown through both caramelization of their sugars and the Maillard reaction with their amino acids.

variants.name: Caramelans, caramelens, caramelins
variants.text: The brown polymers of increasing size and darkness formed as sugar fragments recombine during caramelization.

variants.name: Sugar-specific temperatures
variants.text: The different caramelization temperatures of sugars, with fructose lowest and sucrose around 170 degrees Celsius.

whyItMatters: Caramelization is a fundamental process in cooking and confectionery, transforming plain sugar into complex colour and flavour. It is the basis of caramel candy, sauces, and toppings, gives colour and depth to baked goods, sauces, and roasted foods, and is used to finish dishes from crème brûlée to caramelized fruit. Understanding it lets cooks control the browning of sugar to hit the desired colour and flavour without tipping into bitterness, and it clarifies the distinction from the Maillard reaction, since many browned foods involve both. Caramelization also connects everyday cooking to chemistry, illustrating how heat drives the thermal decomposition of a simple molecule into hundreds of products. Its dependence on temperature and sugar type informs recipes and industrial food production, from candy making to the colouring of foods and beverages. As the process that turns sugar brown and delicious, caramelization is one of the essential browning reactions of the kitchen, alongside the Maillard reaction and distinct from it.

working.text: raise sugar past its caramelization temperature, around 170 degrees Celsius for table sugar, so it melts and decomposes.
let the sugar molecules fragment and recombine into flavour compounds and brown polymers.
control the heating to reach the desired colour and flavour before bitter, burnt compounds form.

limits: Caramelization involves only sugar, so it differs from the Maillard reaction, which requires amino acids as well, and many browned foods involve both, meaning caramelized onions and toasted marshmallows are not pure caramelization examples. The exact caramelization temperatures vary by sugar and by source, so figures like 170 degrees Celsius for sucrose are approximate. It produces a very complex mixture of compounds whose balance depends on temperature, time, and sugar, and overheating produces bitter, burnt flavours, so more browning is not always better. Caramelization also requires relatively high, dry heat and does not occur in watery, low-temperature conditions. So caramelization robustly explains the browning of sugar, understood as a sugar-only process distinct from the Maillard reaction and dependent on careful control of temperature.
misreadings: Caramelization is not the same as the Maillard reaction; caramelization browns sugar alone, while the Maillard reaction also needs amino acids, so browned foods that involve proteins are not pure caramelization. It is not a single simple reaction but a complex thermal breakdown into many compounds. And it is not just about sweetness, since overheating turns caramel bitter and burnt, so treating any browning as caramelization, or caramelization as one simple reaction that only sweetens, misreads the controlled thermal decomposition of sugar into colour and flavour.
origin: A process of non-enzymatic browning in cooking: the thermal decomposition of sugar into brown pigments and flavour compounds, long used in confectionery and distinct from the Maillard reaction.
